title: Rifle Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Rifle wells have a median depth of 80 feet, with typical completed well costs of $10,000-$18,000.
h1: Rifle, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
If you are buying land or a home near Rifle, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells overall, but with meaningful variation from lot to lot. Among permitted wells within five miles, the median reported depth is 80 feet, and the middle half runs from 28 to 160 feet.

That does not guarantee water on a particular parcel. Most permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, and only a fraction of the records include a pump yield or static water level. Use the nearby well history as a screening tool, then confirm the permit, water right, septic layout, and site conditions before closing or building.

sections.heading: Rifle well depth depends on the local ground
sections.html:
Rifle’s reported well depths are concentrated near the shallow end. Fifty-eight percent of the wells with depth records are under 100 feet, while 38% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The middle half of the dataset extends from 28 to 160 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 750 feet.

For a drilling bid, the 80-foot median is a useful starting point, not a promise. A driller may need to go beyond the local middle range if the target formation is tight, fractured, or unproductive. The records identify 2,125 wells with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, compared with only 10 alluvial wells and 16 Wasatch wells. That mix helps explain why neighboring lots can differ.

sections.heading: How much water Rifle wells produce
sections.html:
Reported yields are generally workable for household use, with a median of 13.0 gallons per minute and a middle half from 5.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-five percent of the wells reporting yield make more than 15 gallons per minute, while 38% fall between 5 and 15.

Low production is present but not dominant: 16% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. Those figures describe reported pump tests, not a guarantee for an unbuilt well. Ask for the neighboring permit numbers, completion reports, pump test details, storage capacity, and any history of seasonal shortage before relying on a yield estimate.

sections.heading: Rifle water levels do not show a straight decline
sections.html:
Where static water levels were recorded, the median depth to water is 30 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 14 to 54 feet. That is useful for estimating pumping conditions and planning a well, but it is not the same as a guaranteed production level.

The decade pattern is mixed rather than a simple dropping water table. Median depth to water was 30 feet in the 1990s, 24 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s, and 36 feet in the 2020s. The recent decade is deeper than the prior periods, but only 100 wells report static water levels. Treat this as a limited local signal, not a basin-wide trend or a substitute for checking current neighboring wells.

sections.heading: Rifle’s drilling history and active names
sections.html:
Rifle has a substantial permit history. The records include 2,166 permitted wells, with 1,118 recorded as constructed and 1,376 reporting a total depth. Permitting was most active in the 1990s and 2000s, followed by fewer permits in the 2010s and 2020s. The newest permit year in this dataset is 2025.

Among the most frequently listed drillers are Shelton Drilling Corporation, also shown as Shelton, Wayne, with 535 records; Authorized, shown as Pe, Pg, with 211; and Stoneman Drilling, shown as Stoneman, Frank, with 93. Those names describe the permit record, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references, and who will perform the work before hiring.

sections.heading: What a Rifle well may cost to drill
sections.html:
The local cost model uses mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $4,000 to $6,000 before the rest of the system is installed.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,000 to $18,000. A bid can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more excavation. Ask whether the quote includes water testing, permitting support, casing, grout, pump sizing, storage, trenching, electrical work, and an allowance for unsuccessful drilling.

sections.heading: Rifle risks beyond depth and yield
sections.html:
Water quality deserves its own investigation. Within about 10 miles of Rifle, the map includes 633 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific property, but they are strong reasons to review environmental records and test the well water before purchase.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk remains possible, especially where permits identify fractured bedrock. Also check the location of septic components, reserve areas, driveways, and the proposed building envelope. A well that works for an existing house may not support additional homes, irrigation, or livestock. Confirm the DWR permit and allowed use; domestic and household permits make up 48% of the records, while monitoring wells account for 37%.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Rifle
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then pull permits and completion records for the closest wells rather than relying only on the area median. Compare depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions, construction details, and well uses. Nearby Silt, New Castle, Battlement Mesa, Parachute, Chacra, and Glenwood Springs can provide regional context, but the closest comparable wells matter most.

Before closing, make the seller document the well, pump, pressure system, water quality, and septic approval. For a vacant lot, obtain a driller’s access and depth estimate, verify the legal water use, and lay out the well and septic system together. Colorado DWR permits control important details, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin. Do not assume a good nearby yield transfers to your lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rifle, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Rifle is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 28 to 160 feet, while the deepest record reaches 750 feet. Fifty-eight percent of wells are under 100 feet. These figures help with early budgeting, but fractured-bedrock conditions can make one parcel require a substantially different drilling depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Rifle?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 80-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at about $4,000 to $6,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,000 to $18,000. Site access and unexpected depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Rifle wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median yield of 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-five percent of reported yields exceed 15 gallons per minute. Low production still occurs: 16% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 2% are under 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rifle?
faq.a: The permit map cannot establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, records show 633 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental records before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Are Rifle well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available data does not show a straight decline. Median static water depth was 30 feet in the 1990s, 24 feet in the 2000s, 17 feet in the 2010s, and 36 feet in the 2020s. Only 100 wells report static levels, so the recent deeper figure is a limited local signal rather than proof of a broad, continuing decline.
